news.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
news.summary_raw: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
news.source_text:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.
Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.
news.summary: OpenAI is merging its ChatGPT and Work experiences, introducing a shared usage meter that may cause heavy users to hit limits sooner. The change is rolling out now to a select group of Pro subscribers, with broader deployment planned for December.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your OpenAI account settings this week and monitor your usage meter for the new shared limit. Failure to adjust could mean losing access to advanced models during critical support tasks, impacting incident response times. This directly affects any internal tooling that relies on ChatGPT APIs, so check your integration points in Freshservice or JumpCloud for potential throttling issues.

news.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
news.source_text:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.
news.summary: Adobe’s November 2027 Photoshop update introduces AI features that automatically embed C2PA metadata marking images as AI‑edited, prompting The New York Times to forbid photographers from using the new version to preserve editorial trust.
news.enterprise_use: Review the metadata handling settings in your image assets platform to ensure no C2PA tags are automatically added when using AI tools. This will prevent inadvertent disclosure of AI usage in corporate or client media, mitigating reputational risk. Adjust your asset management workflows to strip or control these tags before publication.

news.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
news.summary_raw: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.
news.source_text:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”

news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to violating the company’s code of conduct during a recent all‑hands meeting, sparking discussion on executive accountability and corporate culture. The incident highlights how leadership actions can affect employee morale and trust, even though it has no direct impact on IT tools or infrastructure.
news.enterprise_use: No immediate action is required for your IT stack. However, consider reviewing your organization’s code of conduct policies to ensure clarity and consistency across all levels. This helps prevent cultural erosion and maintains employee trust, which can indirectly influence productivity and security practices.

news.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
news.summary_raw: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
news.source_text:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.
news.summary: S&P Global Ratings is evaluating a downgrade of Nvidia’s credit rating due to governance concerns and key‑man risk tied to CEO Jensen Huang. The downgrade could increase Nvidia’s borrowing costs, indirectly affecting customers and partners that rely on Nvidia for AI infrastructure financing.

news.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://github.com/lsernau/grh-lean
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50648050
Points: 269

news.source_text:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann
Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the
axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.
- grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at- grh/GUIDE.md.
- grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.
Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.
Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).
The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.
Apache 2.0, Copyright 2026 Anthropic, PBC. See LICENSE, and NOTICE and
ATTRIBUTION.md in each folder.
news.summary: Anthropic released a Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization, built on Mathlib. The repository is a research artifact and not maintained.

In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.
Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:

Use the fonts installed on your computer
Sign documents digitally
Work with local and online files
With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.
Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.
How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:
Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
Log in with your credentials
Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.
Use your own fonts
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!
Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.
Digital signatures and file protection
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.

news.title: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains
news.summary_raw: The FCA warned against “another force of attack” from agents after the company declined a request to work on joint testing ahead of rolling out its personal agent in the UK on Tuesday.
news.source_text:
Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.
“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.
His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says.
Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.
“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.
More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says.
The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.

news.title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
news.source_text:
Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.
Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.
Quick start
You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).
- In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero.
- In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization.
- In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization.
What the numbers mean
The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:
Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.
How we run the benchmarks
We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.
The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.
Inspect and reuse the results
The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.
Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename.
Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.
Join the conversation
Thanks to the AMD team for providing test
news.summary: Hugging Face has released a benchmark dashboard that tracks llama.cpp inference performance on AMD Ryzen and Radeon GPUs, allowing users to compare different models, builds, and quantizations. The public data can be used to evaluate and optimize local AI workloads on AMD hardware.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on the dashboard when planning new AI workloads that might run locally on AMD machines. If your team is considering on‑prem inference for cost or compliance reasons, use the public benchmark results to pick the most efficient model/quantization combination and validate your own builds against the baseline. This can reduce trial‑and‑error and help justify hardware investments.

news.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
news.summary_raw: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
news.source_text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”
“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”
The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”
“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”
But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.
Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.
Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”
Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

news.summary: Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei publicly rebukes claims that AI should relinquish human control, emphasizing the necessity of democratic oversight and human agency. He stresses limits on recursive self‑improvement while acknowledging that Anthropic’s own research increasingly incorporates AI authorship.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on Anthropic’s evolving stance as it may influence future policy discussions around AI governance and internal risk controls. news.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
news.source_text:
Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate
This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.
That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.
Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?
In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.
First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.
The rise of the swarms
We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.
But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.
A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.
